tasks.title: The Withholding Select

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is building the daily Silver pipeline that reads Bronze meter readings, joins to the substations reference table, and writes a slim per-substation summary to Gold. The engineer's first cut works correctly and finishes in about 4 minutes on a 16-core cluster. A teammate notes the pipeline reads 8GB of Parquet for an output that needs only meter_id, substation_id, and daily_kw, and asks the engineer to look at the explain() output before merging.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is building the daily Silver pipeline that reads Bronze meter readings, joins to the substations reference table, and writes a slim per-substation summary to Gold. The engineer's first cut works correctly and finishes in about 4 minutes on a 16-core cluster. A teammate notes the pipeline reads 8GB of Parquet for an output that needs only meter_id, substation_id, and daily_kw, and asks the engineer to look at the explain() output before merging.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Silver-to-Gold step has a 5-minute SLA on the production cluster. The pipeline currently meets the SLA but reads more data than its output requires, leaving no margin when the meter count grows.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (20 rows, 6 columns), substations.csv (6 rows, 4 columns)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

meters = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
subs = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/substations/')

# load everything, then narrow at the end
df = meters.join(subs, 'substation_id', 'left')
df = df.filter(F.col('region') == 'NORTH')
df = df.select('meter_id', 'substation_id', 'daily_kw')
df.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://nordgrid/gold/north_summary/')

evidence.title: Expected Behavior
evidence.content: Read only the three columns needed (meter_id, substation_id, daily_kw) plus the partition column (region) for the filter. Total scan target: ~1.5GB of the 8GB Bronze table.

evidence.title: Observed Behavior
evidence.content: Spark UI shows the FileScan reads 8GB and the ReadSchema lists all 11 columns of the meters table. The filter pushes down (PartitionFilters: [region=NORTH]) but column pruning does not narrow the read.

fields.label: Why does the FileScan read all 11 columns instead of only the three the output uses?
options: The filter on region runs before the select, so Spark must read every column to evaluate the filter expression on the meters DataFrame in the join.
Parquet stores columns together in row groups, so any read of a row group materialises every column the row group contains as part of the scan.
The join is performed on the wide meters DataFrame before the select narrows it, so the read needs every column the join's downstream operators might still reference.
Catalyst inferred the schema from the Parquet footer at planning time and the inferred schema includes all 11 columns regardless of which select calls follow it.
fields.correctAnswer: The join is performed on the wide meters DataFrame before the select narrows it, so the read needs every column the join's downstream operators might still reference.
fields.rationale: Operator order in the chain matters.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Conflates filter pushdown with projection pushdown; the filter pushes down independently of how many columns the read returns.

fields.label: Which single-line edit gives Catalyst the information it needs to prune to three columns at the file scan?
options: Insert a select for the three needed columns plus region on the meters DataFrame BEFORE the join, so the join's input already carries only the columns the output requires.
Move the existing terminal select up so it runs immediately after the filter and before the write, narrowing the projection one stage earlier in the chain.
Add a cache call on the meters DataFrame after the read so Catalyst sees the materialisation point and prunes the columns the cache holds in memory.
Pass a columns list to the spark.read.parquet call so the reader receives the projection at construction and avoids planning the scan over unused columns.
fields.correctAnswer: Insert a select for the three needed columns plus region on the meters DataFrame BEFORE the join, so the join's input already carries only the columns the output requires.
fields.rationale: Putting the projection on meters before the join lets Catalyst see the three-column shape on the left side, and that shape propagates down to the.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats the select's position relative to the filter as the issue; the join is what locks in the column set.

fields.label: The teammate suggests replacing 'meters.join(subs, ...)' with 'meters.select(...).join(subs, ...)'. Which best explains why this change works for column pruning?
options: The select inserted before the join shrinks the join's left-side input row width, which lets the join operator process more rows per executor task without spilling.
The select forces Spark to materialise an intermediate table that the join reads from, breaking the lazy chain and making the pruned columns visible to the planner.
The select adds a Project node after the FileScan and Catalyst pushes the Project down through the FileScan, which lets the reader skip column groups not in the projection.
Catalyst's projection-pushdown rule sees the narrow column set required above the FileScan and configures the Parquet reader to read only those columns from disk.
fields.correctAnswer: Catalyst's projection-pushdown rule sees the narrow column set required above the FileScan and configures the Parquet reader to read only those columns from disk.
fields.rationale: Pruning happens because Catalyst propagates the column requirement down to the data source; the rule examines what is referenced above the scan.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Names a downstream effect (narrower rows) and treats it as the cause of the upstream change (column pruning).

fields.label: After the fix, the engineer reruns and the Spark UI shows ReadSchema: [meter_id, substation_id, daily_kw, region]. Why does region appear even though the output does not use it?
options: Region is the table's partition column and Parquet stores the partition value in the file path; the reader includes it free without reading any column data from the files.
Region is needed at planning time to evaluate the filter expression, so Catalyst keeps it in the read schema even after the select that excludes it from the join's output.
Region was selected indirectly because the substations DataFrame contains a region column with the same name and the join key resolution pulled it into the meters scan.
Region is included in the read schema as a side effect of partition discovery; Spark added it to the schema during the directory listing that precedes the file scan.
fields.correctAnswer: Region is the table's partition column and Parquet stores the partition value in the file path; the reader includes it free without reading any column data from the files.
fields.rationale: , region=NORTH) and the reader gets them by parsing the path, not by reading file content.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats the filter as if it ran at the scan; partition filters resolve before any file is opened.

fields.label: Suppose the engineer adds a withColumn that derives reading_grade from daily_kw before the terminal select. What happens to the read schema?
options: The withColumn introduces a Project node that Catalyst does not push past the FileScan, so the read schema falls back to all 11 columns of the meters Parquet table.
The withColumn shifts the scan to read all columns referenced anywhere in the chain, which adds reading_grade as a virtual column and triggers a full scan in the process.
The read schema is unchanged because reading_grade depends only on daily_kw, which is already in the projection, and Catalyst's pruning sees the same minimal column set.
The read schema gains reading_grade because Catalyst includes derived columns in the FileScan's projection so the executor can compute them as part of the read step.
fields.correctAnswer: The read schema is unchanged because reading_grade depends only on daily_kw, which is already in the projection, and Catalyst's pruning sees the same minimal column set.
fields.rationale: Pruning tracks the columns the chain actually reads, not the columns it derives.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Asserts that withColumn breaks projection pushdown when it does not; the rule still fires.

tasks.title: The Filter That Stayed Put

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is debugging a Bronze-to-Silver pipeline that scans 12GB instead of the 800MB the team expects. The Bronze table is partitioned by date, and the engineer's query is supposed to read only one date. The pipeline produces correct output but reads sixteen times more data than needed. A quick look at the explain() shows the date predicate appears in the Filter node above the FileScan but does not appear in PartitionFilters at the scan itself.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is debugging a Bronze-to-Silver pipeline that scans 12GB instead of the 800MB the team expects. The Bronze table is partitioned by date, and the engineer's query is supposed to read only one date. The pipeline produces correct output but reads sixteen times more data than needed. A quick look at the explain() shows the date predicate appears in the Filter node above the FileScan but does not appear in PartitionFilters at the scan itself.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Bronze layer is read by twelve downstream pipelines daily. Read amplification on this pipeline costs cluster minutes that show up on the team's monthly bill, and the missing partition pruning is the difference between a 25-second scan and a 6-minute scan.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Bronze layer is partitioned by date)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

target_date = '2026-03-15'

bronze = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
bronze = bronze.withColumn(
    'is_target',
    F.when(F.col('date') == target_date, F.lit(True)).otherwise(F.lit(False))
)
silver = bronze.filter(F.col('is_target')).select('meter_id', 'date', 'daily_kw')
silver.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://nordgrid/silver/meters/2026-03-15/')

evidence.title: Expected Behavior
evidence.content: Catalyst pushes the date predicate down to the FileScan as a PartitionFilter so only the date=2026-03-15 directory is read (~800MB).

evidence.title: Observed Behavior
evidence.content: PartitionFilters is empty in the plan. ReadSchema includes is_target. The scan reads all 30 daily directories (~12GB) and the filter applies after the read.

fields.label: Why does Catalyst fail to push the date predicate down to PartitionFilters?
options: The filter checks is_target rather than date, and is_target is a derived column that does not exist on the Parquet file system, so Catalyst has no partition path to match the predicate against during planning.

The filter operator runs after the withColumn step, and Catalyst applies pushdown rules in the order the chain declares them rather than reordering filters past intermediate withColumn steps that hold on to the predicate.

The when expression that defines is_target wraps the date comparison inside a conditional, and Catalyst does not unwrap conditional expressions to extract pushable predicates from inside the branch arms during planning.

The filter compares against a Python variable target_date that the planner sees as a runtime value, and pushdown to PartitionFilters works only on literal expressions known at compile time inside the filter call itself.
fields.correctAnswer: The filter operator runs after the withColumn step, and Catalyst applies pushdown rules in the order the chain declares them rather than reordering filters past intermediate withColumn steps that hold on to the predicate.
fields.rationale: When Catalyst processes the chain, it tries to push pushable predicates down through projections.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Names a true fact about is_target but blames the file system rather than the chain order that hides the underlying date predicate.

fields.label: Which single edit restores partition pruning without changing the output of the pipeline?
options: Replace the when expression with a coalesce of date and a literal, then use the result column as the filter predicate so Catalyst sees a stable column reference at the filter step.
Move the withColumn step to run after the select so Catalyst's pushdown rule applies to a chain in which the filter sits directly above the FileScan with no intermediate projection.
Replace the existing filter with a direct predicate on date, dropping the is_target derivation entirely; the comparison against the partition column is what enables pushdown to PartitionFilters.
Add a hint that requests partition pruning on the date column before the withColumn runs, which gives Catalyst an explicit instruction to extract the predicate from the conditional.
fields.correctAnswer: Replace the existing filter with a direct predicate on date, dropping the is_target derivation entirely; the comparison against the partition column is what enables pushdown to PartitionFilters.
fields.rationale: The cleanest fix is to filter directly on date because that is the partition column.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats coalesce as a way to expose a predicate; it produces a different expression that is also not pushable.

fields.label: After the fix, the engineer wants to keep an is_target boolean for an audit log that the team writes alongside the silver output. Which placement preserves partition pruning?
options: Add the withColumn after the partition filter on date so the derivation runs only on the rows that survive the pruned scan and the filter still pushes down at the FileScan.
Add the withColumn before the filter and add a second filter on date in addition to the is_target filter so Catalyst sees the pushable predicate at the filter step alongside the derived one.
Add the withColumn after the filter on is_target so the derivation is computed only after pruning has happened, matching the chain order Catalyst inspects when applying its rule.
Add the withColumn before the read by passing it as a transform option to spark.read.parquet so the derivation happens inside the reader and never participates in the filter chain at all.
fields.correctAnswer: Add the withColumn after the partition filter on date so the derivation runs only on the rows that survive the pruned scan and the filter still pushes down at the FileScan.
fields.rationale: Putting the derivation after the filter means the partition pruning happens first and only the surviving rows feed the withColumn.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Reaches for two filters when one (after the derivation) is the same fix proposed for the previous question.

fields.label: The fix is shipped. PartitionFilters now shows [date=2026-03-15] and the scan reads ~800MB. Which other plan field most directly confirms the pruning worked at the directory level?
options: ReadSchema, which now lists only the columns the select projects, confirming Spark narrowed both the column projection and the partition reading at the scan operator level.
Number of partitions read, shown as the count of input directories the FileScan opened; one partition read confirms the planner skipped the other twenty-nine date directories on disk.
PushedFilters, which now lists the date equality predicate, confirming Spark sent the filter to the Parquet reader at the file level rather than only at the directory listing step.
Output rows estimate, shown as one-thirtieth of the original Bronze row count, confirming the cost-based optimiser reduced its row count estimate to match the pruned partition input.
fields.correctAnswer: Number of partitions read, shown as the count of input directories the FileScan opened; one partition read confirms the planner skipped the other twenty-nine date directories on disk.
fields.rationale: The directory-skipping evidence sits in the per-scan input counter that the SQL DAG reports under the FileScan; one input directory means twenty-nine.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Conflates column pruning evidence with partition pruning evidence; both are pruning but at different layers.

tasks.title: Did the Pushdown Happen?

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is comparing two near-identical queries against the Bronze meters Parquet table. The two queries return the same rows but the runtimes differ by a factor of nine. The team's lead asks the engineer to read the explain() output for each and identify which one pushed the predicate down to the Parquet reader and which one did not. The Bronze table is partitioned by date and stored as plain Parquet (not Delta).
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is comparing two near-identical queries against the Bronze meters Parquet table. The two queries return the same rows but the runtimes differ by a factor of nine. The team's lead asks the engineer to read the explain() output for each and identify which one pushed the predicate down to the Parquet reader and which one did not. The Bronze table is partitioned by date and stored as plain Parquet (not Delta).

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The slow query is on a developer's hot-loop iteration path. Cutting it from 45 seconds to 5 seconds saves the developer enough time across a working day that the team treats it as a productivity-grade optimisation, not just a performance one.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Bronze partitioned by date)

evidence.label: Query A
evidence.content:
df = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
result = df.filter(df.date == '2026-03-15').filter(df.daily_kw > 1000).select('meter_id', 'daily_kw')

evidence.label: Query B
evidence.content:
df = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
df = df.withColumn('daily_kw_norm', df.daily_kw / 1000.0)
result = df.filter(df.date == '2026-03-15').filter(df.daily_kw_norm > 1.0).select('meter_id', 'daily_kw_norm')

evidence.label: Plan A
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [meter_id, daily_kw]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw) AND (daily_kw > 1000.0))
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [meter_id, daily_kw, date]
         Batched: true, DataFilters: [isnotnull(daily_kw), (daily_kw > 1000.0)],
         Format: Parquet, PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(date), (date = 2026-03-15)],
         PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw, 1000.0)],
         ReadSchema: struct<meter_id:string, daily_kw:double>

evidence.label: Plan B
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [meter_id, (daily_kw / 1000.0) AS daily_kw_norm]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw) AND ((daily_kw / 1000.0) > 1.0))
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [meter_id, daily_kw, date]
         Batched: true, DataFilters: [isnotnull(daily_kw)],
         Format: Parquet, PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(date), (date = 2026-03-15)],
         PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw)],
         ReadSchema: struct<meter_id:string, daily_kw:double>

fields.label: Which plan field tells you the daily_kw threshold predicate was sent into the Parquet reader for query A?
options: PushedFilters lists GreaterThan(daily_kw, 1000.0), which is the form the Parquet reader interprets to skip row groups whose statistics show no values can satisfy the predicate at file read time.
DataFilters lists the daily_kw threshold expression, which records that the Filter operator above the scan applies the predicate to each row Spark reads from the Parquet files.
PartitionFilters lists the predicate alongside the date predicate, which records that Spark uses both predicates together at the directory listing step before any file is opened.
The Project node references daily_kw, which records that Spark reads the column out of the Parquet files and applies the threshold during the columnar-to-row conversion at the scan boundary.
fields.correctAnswer: PushedFilters lists GreaterThan(daily_kw, 1000.0), which is the form the Parquet reader interprets to skip row groups whose statistics show no values can satisfy the predicate at file read time.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters is the field that lists predicates sent into the data source, where the Parquet reader can use min/max statistics in the row-group.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Confuses the row-by-row filter the operator applies with the row-group skipping the reader applies; DataFilters documents the former.

fields.label: Why does plan B not list a daily_kw_norm threshold in PushedFilters?
options: The Parquet reader rejects predicates with floating-point operands because comparison semantics differ between the file format and the JVM, so divisions like daily_kw_norm are evaluated only above the scan.
The Parquet reader accepts predicates only on columns that exist as fields in the file schema, and daily_kw_norm is a derived column that does not exist in the meters Parquet files at the read step.

Catalyst applies pushdown only to the first filter in the chain after the scan, and daily_kw_norm appears in the second filter, so the rule has already finished running by the time it reaches the second filter.

PushedFilters tracks predicates that survived the Catalyst rule that combines adjacent filters into one, and the daily_kw_norm filter merged into the date filter, removing it from the pushable predicate set.
fields.correctAnswer: Catalyst applies pushdown only to the first filter in the chain after the scan, and daily_kw_norm appears in the second filter, so the rule has already finished running by the time it reaches the second filter.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters can only carry predicates that reference columns the data source actually has.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Invents a floating-point semantics block; the reader handles double comparisons routinely.

fields.label: Both plans show ReadSchema: struct<meter_id:string, daily_kw:double>. What does this confirm?
options: Both queries projected the date column out of the read because the partition filter consumed it during planning, leaving only the columns referenced by the surviving operators above the scan.
Both queries narrowed the Parquet column read to the two columns each one actually uses; column pruning works for both even though plan B has the additional derived column above the scan.
Both queries produced identical physical plans because Catalyst's rules normalise away the syntactic difference between filtering on daily_kw directly and filtering on daily_kw_norm in the chain.
Both queries forced the reader to load only daily_kw and meter_id, but the Parquet column index is consulted at read time using the values listed in PushedFilters before the load happens.
fields.correctAnswer: Both queries narrowed the Parquet column read to the two columns each one actually uses; column pruning works for both even though plan B has the additional derived column above the scan.
fields.rationale: ReadSchema records the columns the reader materialises from the files.Both queries list meter_id and daily_kw, so column pruning fired in each case.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Reaches for partition projection logic when ReadSchema documents the file column read.

fields.label: Which line in plan A confirms that only the 2026-03-15 directory was opened, regardless of how the file-level pushdown applied?
options: The DataFilters line, which carries the predicate alongside the row-group statistics that the FileScan operator uses to decide which directories to list during planning.
The PartitionFilters line, which records the predicates Spark evaluated against the partition values encoded in the directory paths before opening any files at all.
The ReadSchema line, which lists only the non-partition columns and confirms by omission that the date partition column was resolved at the directory listing step.
The PushedFilters line on the daily_kw predicate, which confirms by sequence that the date predicate was evaluated earlier and limited the listing to the 2026-03-15 directory.
fields.correctAnswer: The PartitionFilters line, which records the predicates Spark evaluated against the partition values encoded in the directory paths before opening any files at all.
fields.rationale: Directory-level pruning is what PartitionFilters records.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Maps row-group statistics to directory listing; the two operate at different layers.

fields.label: Suppose the engineer rewrites query B to use 'daily_kw > 1000.0' instead of 'daily_kw_norm > 1.0' (keeping the withColumn that derives daily_kw_norm for the output). What changes in plan B?
options: PushedFilters loses the IsNotNull entry because the rewritten predicate no longer triggers the null check that the Parquet reader injects when comparing a derived column to a literal of a different precision.

The Project node above the Filter expands to include the derivation expression so the daily_kw_norm column is materialised after the threshold filter runs against the original daily_kw column at the scan.
ReadSchema stays the same because the read still needs daily_kw and meter_id and the change touches only the predicate the reader gets, not the columns it materialises during the scan.
PushedFilters gains a new entry for the daily_kw threshold matching the entry in plan A; the rewrite exposes the predicate on the actual file column instead of on the derived one.
fields.correctAnswer: PushedFilters gains a new entry for the daily_kw threshold matching the entry in plan A; the rewrite exposes the predicate on the actual file column instead of on the derived one.
fields.rationale: The rewrite places the threshold on daily_kw, which the file schema does have, so PushedFilters now matches plan A.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Invents a null-check behaviour tied to derived columns that the reader does not implement that way.

tasks.title: Counting Shuffles in a Five-Step Plan

description.context: A NordGrid engineer wrote a 30-line Silver pipeline that reads meters, joins to substations, computes a per-region daily total, deduplicates against a quality lookup, and writes a Gold table. The pipeline finishes in 11 minutes. The engineer suspects one of the operations is causing a shuffle that is not strictly necessary. The lead asks the engineer to read the physical plan and count Exchange nodes, name what each one is for, and identify which one (if any) could be eliminated.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer wrote a 30-line Silver pipeline that reads meters, joins to substations, computes a per-region daily total, deduplicates against a quality lookup, and writes a Gold table. The pipeline finishes in 11 minutes. The engineer suspects one of the operations is causing a shuffle that is not strictly necessary. The lead asks the engineer to read the physical plan and count Exchange nodes, name what each one is for, and identify which one (if any) could be eliminated.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: Every shuffle in this pipeline writes between 600MB and 4GB of data through the network and back to disk on the cluster. Eliminating one unnecessary shuffle saves five to seven minutes of stage time and the corresponding executor memory pressure.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv, substations.csv (small reference table)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
meters = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
subs = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/substations/')
quality = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/quality/')

joined = meters.join(subs, 'substation_id', 'left')
filtered = joined.filter(F.col('region') == 'NORTH')
agg = filtered.groupBy('region', 'date').agg(F.sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'))
deduped = agg.join(quality, ['region', 'date'], 'left').dropDuplicates(['region', 'date'])
deduped.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://nordgrid/gold/north_daily/')

evidence.label: Physical Plan
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(7) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)        [E3]
   +- *(6) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[partial_first])
      +- *(6) Project [region, date, total_kw, quality_flag]
         +- *(6) SortMergeJoin [region, date], [region, date], LeftOuter
            :- *(3) Sort [region, date]
            :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)        [E2]
            :     +- *(2) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[sum(daily_kw)])
            :        +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)  [E1]
            :           +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw)])
            :              +- *(1) BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id], [substation_id], LeftOuter, BuildRight
            :                 :- *(1) Filter (region = NORTH)
            :                 :  +- FileScan parquet meters
            :                 +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode             [B1]
            :                    +- FileScan parquet subs
            +- *(5) Sort [region, date]
               +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)        [E4]
                  +- FileScan parquet quality

fields.label: How many shuffle Exchange nodes (excluding the broadcast exchange) does the plan contain?
options: Three Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan, with one for each of the user-visible operations the chain expresses: the groupBy step, the join step, and the dropDuplicates step at the end.

Four Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan: the partial sum produces one, the join requires one on each side of the sort-merge step, and the dropDuplicates produces one before the final aggregate.
Two Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan, since Catalyst combined the groupBy and the dropDuplicates into a single shuffle stage and reused the post-aggregate distribution.
Five Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan, since each of the read steps and each of the join steps issues its own Exchange in the SortMergeJoin sequence above the partial aggregates.
fields.correctAnswer: Four Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan: the partial sum produces one, the join requires one on each side of the sort-merge step, and the dropDuplicates produces one before the final aggregate.
fields.rationale: The plan shows four Exchange nodes labelled E1–E4.E1 sits above the partial aggregate of the groupBy.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Counts at the source-code-operation level, not the plan-operator level; the join contributes two Exchanges, not one.

fields.label: Which Exchange (E1, E2, E3, or E4) corresponds to the dropDuplicates step in the source code?
options: E2 corresponds to dropDuplicates because the chain emits the deduplication after the aggregate and the second Exchange in the plan tree appears immediately above the partial aggregate at that level of the chain.

E3 corresponds to dropDuplicates because Catalyst implements dropDuplicates as a HashAggregate with first-on-each-key semantics, and E3 sits below the outer HashAggregate that produces the final output.
E4 corresponds to dropDuplicates because it sits on the right side of the SortMergeJoin and the deduplication needs to align both sides on the deduplication key before the join produces output.
E1 corresponds to dropDuplicates because the partial aggregate at the lowest level of the plan represents the deduplication step that runs before any other shuffle in the pipeline executes.
fields.correctAnswer: E1 corresponds to dropDuplicates because the partial aggregate at the lowest level of the plan represents the deduplication step that runs before any other shuffle in the pipeline executes.
fields.rationale: Reading the plan carefully, the outer HashAggregate at the top has functions=[] (no aggregation function), which is how Catalyst implements.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Picks E2 because dropDuplicates is the second-to-last source operation, conflating source order with plan order.

fields.label: The engineer notices that the dropDuplicates step uses the same key as the groupBy step. Which observation about this redundancy is correct?

fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Names a real but minor cost at write time; the read-side granularity loss is the binding issue.

fields.label: If the team adopts the DateType change, which existing piece of consumer code would still work unchanged after the cast?

Casting at Bronze ensures the partition column is a typed value that participates in partition pruning across all consumers, while casting at Silver leaves the Bronze partition layer indexed by the original string form.

fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Names the per-read cost as the binding argument; the partition layer is more impactful than the per-read CPU.

evidence.title: Incremental Write Pattern
evidence.content: Each 30-minute batch appends a small partition write (1-3 files) into the current date directory.

evidence.label: Candidate Remedies
evidence.content:
[
  "Repartition the DataFrame to 1 partition before each write so the writer produces one file per write call",
  "Coalesce the DataFrame to a target number of partitions before each write to limit file count per batch",
  "Raise spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile so the writer combines incoming rows into fewer larger files",
  "Run a separate compaction job nightly that rewrites each date directory as a small number of larger files"

fields.label: Why do 24,000 small files cost more on read than 1,000 medium-to-large files holding the same data?
options: Each file open requires a separate task in the cluster's scheduler, and 24,000 tasks introduce coordination overhead that grows non-linearly when tasks finish faster than the driver can dispatch the next ones at scale.

Each file open issues a metadata round-trip to object storage and parses the Parquet footer; these costs are largely per-file rather than per-byte and dominate the scan when files sit well below the read-block size.

Small files miss the read-buffer pool because the Parquet reader caches whole files in memory, so 24,000 files pressure the buffer pool harder than 1,000 files that fit comfortably in the cache during a scan.

Small files break the columnar layout because each file holds too few rows for the row-group structure to populate column statistics, which the planner uses for pruning at the scan operator level on every read.
fields.correctAnswer: Each file open issues a metadata round-trip to object storage and parses the Parquet footer; these costs are largely per-file rather than per-byte and dominate the scan when files sit well below the read-block size.
fields.rationale: Storage round-trips and footer parses are paid once per file regardless of size.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Names scheduler coordination as the dominant cost; it contributes but is much smaller than the per-file I/O on object storage.

fields.label: Which proposed remedy addresses the root cause without introducing a new problem on the write path?
options: Repartitioning to 1 partition per write produces one file per write call but funnels the entire 30-minute batch through a single executor, which makes the write step a serial bottleneck on every batch.

Coalescing to a small target number of partitions limits the file count per batch but produces fewer files per write than the cluster could in parallel, leaving a fraction of the file count problem in place across days.

Raising spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile lets the writer combine more rows per file at write time, but the 30-minute batch only produces enough rows for a single small file already, so the threshold does not change file count.

A nightly compaction job rewrites each date directory as a few larger files, leaving the 30-minute write path untouched and addressing the historical small-file accumulation that the readers hit during the audit run.
fields.correctAnswer: A nightly compaction job rewrites each date directory as a few larger files, leaving the 30-minute write path untouched and addressing the historical small-file accumulation that the readers hit during the audit run.
fields.rationale: Compaction targets the accumulated state of historical files without coupling to the write path.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Picks single-partition write for predictable file count; pays a serial-write cost on every batch.

fields.label: After the compaction job runs for a week, the engineer notices that today's date directory still has 48 small files. Why?
options: The compaction job runs nightly and the current day's directory has not yet been compacted; today's files will be merged when tonight's job runs against the previous day's directory after the daily roll boundary.

The compaction job is configured to skip the current day's directory because compacting an actively-written directory risks lock contention with the 30-minute writer's appends; only closed-day directories are compacted on each job run.

The compaction job skips files smaller than its target file size because rewriting them costs more than the read saving they provide; today's files have not yet accumulated to the size threshold the job uses.
The compaction job compacts only files whose modification time is older than a configured age; today's files were written within the age window and are excluded from the current job run by design.
fields.correctAnswer: The compaction job is configured to skip the current day's directory because compacting an actively-written directory risks lock contention with the 30-minute writer's appends; only closed-day directories are compacted on each job run.
fields.rationale: Compacting a directory that is being actively appended risks file-handle lock contention with the writer; the safe pattern is to compact yesterday's.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Names the correct visible behaviour but credits scheduling rather than the safety reason behind the schedule.

fields.label: An engineer asks whether maxRecordsPerFile is the right setting to manage going forward. Which statement is correct about its role?
options: maxRecordsPerFile sets an upper bound on the number of records per file at write time, splitting large output partitions into multiple files; it does not combine small batches into larger files at the write step.

maxRecordsPerFile sets a target number of records per file that the writer aims for, combining small input batches into larger output files when the target is set above the per-batch row count at write time.

maxRecordsPerFile sets a soft target that the writer respects when the cluster has spare capacity but ignores when the executor pool is saturated, leading to inconsistent file sizes across batches in production.
maxRecordsPerFile sets the row-group size inside each Parquet file, so raising it produces fewer row groups per file rather than fewer files per batch in the write output.
fields.correctAnswer: maxRecordsPerFile sets an upper bound on the number of records per file at write time, splitting large output partitions into multiple files; it does not combine small batches into larger files at the write step.
fields.rationale: maxRecordsPerFile is an upper bound the writer respects when an output partition would otherwise produce a single very large file.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Inverts the role; maxRecordsPerFile is a splitter, not a combiner.

fields.label: The engineer ships compaction. Six months later, the audit job still reads more files than the engineer expected. Which check is the right next step?
options: Read the compaction job's run log to confirm it has been running on schedule and check for partitions it skipped or failed to compact, since long-running compaction setups can silently miss days when the underlying job fails partially.

Inspect the per-partition file count on the Silver directory, since incremental writes between compactions accumulate small files and the file count steady state depends on the compaction-run-to-write-frequency ratio.

Re-run the compaction job manually on the current month to confirm it produces the expected file count, then compare against historical compactions to see whether the job's behaviour has drifted across its operational lifetime.

Profile the audit job's listing step in the Spark UI to see how much time goes to listing versus reading, and use the ratio to decide whether the file count is the binding cost or whether another step in the audit is the slow part.
fields.correctAnswer: Inspect the per-partition file count on the Silver directory, since incremental writes between compactions accumulate small files and the file count steady state depends on the compaction-run-to-write-frequency ratio.
fields.rationale: Confirm the symptom directly: count how many files each date directory currently holds.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Goes to the run log without first confirming the count; the log is one cause of count drift, not the only one.

tasks.title: The Regex UDF That Could Be a Function

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver pipeline that runs in 14 minutes. Profiling shows that 9 of those minutes are spent inside a Python UDF that extracts a four-character station code from each meter_id. Every meter_id has the form 'MTR-WXYZ-12345678' where WXYZ is the station code. The UDF compiles a regex once at module load and applies it row by row. The team's lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements and pick the one that preserves the semantics with the largest performance gain.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver pipeline that runs in 14 minutes. Profiling shows that 9 of those minutes are spent inside a Python UDF that extracts a four-character station code from each meter_id. Every meter_id has the form 'MTR-WXYZ-12345678' where WXYZ is the station code. The UDF compiles a regex once at module load and applies it row by row. The team's lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements and pick the one that preserves the semantics with the largest performance gain.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Silver pipeline runs every 30 minutes and feeds three downstream consumers. Cutting the 9-minute UDF segment to under 1 minute would bring total pipeline time from 14 minutes back under the 7-minute target the team set when the pipeline was first written.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (meter_id format 'MTR-WXYZ-12345678'; station code is positions 5-8 inclusive, zero-indexed; about 500,000 rows per daily Silver run)

evidence.label: Udf Implementation
evidence.content:
import re
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
from pyspark.sql.types import StringType

_pattern = re.compile(r'^MTR-([A-Z]{4})-\d{8}$')

@udf(returnType=StringType())
def extract_station_code(meter_id):
    if meter_id is None:
        return None
    m = _pattern.match(meter_id)
    return m.group(1) if m else None

df = df.withColumn('station_code', extract_station_code('meter_id'))

evidence.label: Candidate Replacements
evidence.content:
[
  "regexp_extract(col('meter_id'), r'^MTR-([A-Z]{4})-\\d{8}$', 1)",
  "substring(col('meter_id'), 5, 4) — positional substring, 1-indexed",
  "split(col('meter_id'), '-').getItem(1)",
  "A different UDF written in Pandas with @pandas_udf for vectorised execution"
]

fields.label: Why does the existing UDF take 9 of the pipeline's 14 minutes despite the precompiled regex?
options: The regex match itself is the expensive step because Python's re module backtracks on each row, and 500,000 rows of backtracking accumulate to the 9 minutes the engineer observes in the profiler.

The UDF allocates a fresh Python string object for the matched group on each row, and the garbage collection that runs across 500,000 allocated objects is what the profiler reports as the bulk of the UDF time.
The UDF holds the Python global interpreter lock for the regex evaluation, which serialises across executor cores and pushes the parallel pipeline into a serial section that lasts 9 minutes.

Each UDF call serialises the row to Python, runs the regex, and serialises the result back to the JVM; the per-row Python boundary crossing is what dominates and is independent of how the regex itself is implemented.
fields.correctAnswer: Each UDF call serialises the row to Python, runs the regex, and serialises the result back to the JVM; the per-row Python boundary crossing is what dominates and is independent of how the regex itself is implemented.
fields.rationale: Spark UDFs that take Python functions cross the language boundary on every row.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Pins the cost on regex backtracking; for this pattern there is no backtracking and the regex itself is fast.

fields.label: Which of the four candidates is the right replacement?
options: The split-then-getItem approach is the right replacement because it expresses the same string operation in a structural way that the planner can apply column-wise without per-row Python work in the executor.

The regexp_extract built-in is the right replacement because it expresses the same regex pattern at the Catalyst level, runs in the JVM without a Python boundary, and preserves the validation against the format that the original UDF performed.

The substring built-in is the right replacement because it is the simplest expression that yields the four-character station code, and simpler is better for a code that follows a fixed positional pattern.

The pandas_udf rewrite is the right replacement because vectorised UDFs cross the Python boundary in batches rather than per row, which gives most of the performance gain without changing the regex logic at all.
fields.correctAnswer: The regexp_extract built-in is the right replacement because it expresses the same regex pattern at the Catalyst level, runs in the JVM without a Python boundary, and preserves the validation against the format that the original UDF performed.
fields.rationale: Of the four candidates, only the regex-based built-in keeps the format check that the original Python implementation gave for free; it runs as a JVM.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Picks split for its structural feel; works but skips the format validation.

fields.label: Why is substring(col('meter_id'), 5, 4) NOT the right replacement here, even though it works on every well-formed meter_id?
options: substring would silently produce a four-character slice for any malformed meter_id (e.g., a meter_id missing the prefix), where the original UDF returns null on a regex mismatch; the substring loses the validation the regex provided.

substring uses 1-indexed positions in Spark's expression engine and the engineer would have to remember the off-by-one convention each time the function appears in the codebase, which is fragile against later edits.

substring on a column of variable-length strings returns null when the string is shorter than the start position, and the meter_id field allows null values that the substring path treats inconsistently with the regex path used by the UDF.

substring requires the engineer to declare the length of the slice as a literal at planning time, which the regex approach handles dynamically through the capturing group's lookup at runtime against the variable input length.
fields.correctAnswer: substring would silently produce a four-character slice for any malformed meter_id (e.g., a meter_id missing the prefix), where the original UDF returns null on a regex mismatch; the substring loses the validation the regex provided.
fields.rationale: Format validation is what the regex was buying.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Names a real but minor concern (1-indexing) as the binding reason; the binding reason is validation loss.

fields.label: After replacing the UDF with regexp_extract, the engineer measures the new pipeline at 5 minutes total. Which of the original UDF's costs is GONE in the new version?
options: The regex compilation cost, since regexp_extract precompiles the pattern once at planning time and caches it for the duration of the query without re-parsing the pattern on each row of the DataFrame.
The driver-to-executor task dispatch overhead, since the UDF was running on the driver in the original implementation and the built-in expression runs natively on the executor for each partition.

The Python boundary crossing per row, since regexp_extract runs as a Catalyst expression in the JVM and Spark no longer serialises each row to a Python interpreter and back to the JVM during the column derivation.

The garbage collection pressure from the per-row string allocations, since the JVM's string interning pool reuses the four-character station codes across rows in a way the Python interpreter could not match for the original UDF.
fields.correctAnswer: The Python boundary crossing per row, since regexp_extract runs as a Catalyst expression in the JVM and Spark no longer serialises each row to a Python interpreter and back to the JVM during the column derivation.
fields.rationale: The boundary crossing was the dominant cost (per Q1) and regexp_extract removes it by running in the JVM.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Reaches for compilation cost as the saving; both implementations precompile.

tasks.title: When the UDF Is Genuinely Needed

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver enrichment pipeline that calls an external pricing service to compute a tariff-adjusted reading for each row. The UDF wraps an HTTPS request to the pricing service's per-lookup endpoint, which accepts customer_type and region as inputs and returns a price multiplier. The pricing service is owned by another team and is the only authoritative source for the multiplier values. The pipeline runs in 38 minutes, and the lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements proposed by a junior teammate.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver enrichment pipeline that calls an external pricing service to compute a tariff-adjusted reading for each row. The UDF wraps an HTTPS request to the pricing service's per-lookup endpoint, which accepts customer_type and region as inputs and returns a price multiplier. The pricing service is owned by another team and is the only authoritative source for the multiplier values. The pipeline runs in 38 minutes, and the lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements proposed by a junior teammate.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The pricing service has rate limits (200 requests per second) and the multiplier values change infrequently (a few times per quarter when tariff schedules update). The Silver pipeline runs every 30 minutes against 500,000 rows; calling the service per row exceeds the rate limit and is also wasteful given how rarely values change.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (500,000 rows; columns include customer_type and region; the (customer_type, region) pair has cardinality 16 — 4 customer types × 4 regions)

evidence.label: Udf Implementation
Candidate Replacements
evidence.content:
[
  "Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a small Spark DataFrame at the top of the pipeline and broadcast-join it on (customer_type, region)",
  "Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a Python dict, broadcast the dict to executors, and rewrite the UDF to look up from the dict instead of calling the service",
  "Convert the UDF to mapInPandas so HTTPS calls run in batches per partition rather than per row",
  "Leave the UDF in place but raise the executor count to a level where the rate limit is no longer the binding cost"
]

fields.label: What is the dominant cost of the current implementation, and is it the same kind of cost as POJ5.1's UDF?
options: The dominant cost is the Python boundary crossing per row, the same kind of cost as POJ5.1; replacing with a built-in expression would eliminate it the same way regexp_extract did in the previous exercise.

The dominant cost is the HTTPS call latency per row at 500,000 rows, which is a network-bound cost rather than a CPU-bound or boundary-crossing cost; the previous exercise's pattern does not apply here.

The dominant cost is the network round-trip per row, which is fundamentally external to Spark; the previous exercise's pattern does not apply because the UDF itself is fast and the slowness is in the service call.

The dominant cost is the JSON parsing on each response, which Spark's built-in JSON expressions could replace; the boundary-crossing pattern from the previous exercise applies indirectly through the parse step.
fields.correctAnswer: The dominant cost is the network round-trip per row, which is fundamentally external to Spark; the previous exercise's pattern does not apply because the UDF itself is fast and the slowness is in the service call.
fields.rationale: The 38 minutes are dominated by waiting on a remote service, not by Python language overhead.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Reaches for the previous exercise's lesson without checking whether the cost shape is the same.

fields.label: Which of the four candidates is the right replacement?
options: Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a small Spark DataFrame at the top of the pipeline and broadcast-join it on the customer_type and region keys; 16 lookups happen once per run and the per-row HTTPS call disappears.

Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a Python dict and broadcast the dict to executors; the per-row UDF still runs but reads from local memory instead of calling the service, eliminating the network cost while keeping the UDF code structure.

Convert the UDF to mapInPandas so the HTTPS calls run in batches per partition; the per-row latency becomes per-batch latency, and the rate limit is respected because each partition issues one request per its set of unique pairs.

Leave the UDF in place and scale the executor count so the rate limit is no longer the binding cost; the simplest change in code preserves the existing structure and only adjusts the cluster configuration to fit the workload.
fields.correctAnswer: Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a small Spark DataFrame at the top of the pipeline and broadcast-join it on the customer_type and region keys; 16 lookups happen once per run and the per-row HTTPS call disappears.
fields.rationale: Sixteen unique input combinations and quarter-changing values mean the right structural move is to load all 16 in advance and turn the external.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Picks the dict-broadcast approach for keeping the UDF; introduces unnecessary boundary crossing.

fields.label: The teammate proposes the broadcast-dict approach (option B). What is the strongest argument for picking the broadcast-join approach over the broadcast-dict approach?
options: The broadcast-join approach avoids serialising and deserialising the dict on every partition, which adds a one-time cost per task that the broadcast-join pattern handles inside Catalyst's join operator without per-task overhead.

The broadcast-join approach gives Catalyst visibility into the join, which means the join statistics and the dynamic filtering rules apply; the broadcast-dict approach hides the lookup inside a UDF that the optimiser cannot reason about.

The broadcast-join approach keeps the multiplier in a typed Spark column from the start, while the broadcast-dict approach materialises it through a Python UDF that adds the boundary-crossing cost POJ5.1 was about.

The broadcast-join approach scales to larger lookup tables because Catalyst can choose to fall back to a sort-merge join when the table grows beyond the broadcast threshold; the dict approach hard-codes the broadcast model regardless of size.
fields.correctAnswer: The broadcast-join approach scales to larger lookup tables because Catalyst can choose to fall back to a sort-merge join when the table grows beyond the broadcast threshold; the dict approach hard-codes the broadcast model regardless of size.
fields.rationale: Lookup-table size grows over time.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Names a real but smaller cost (dict ser/deser per task); the scalability argument is structurally larger.

fields.label: Suppose the multiplier service returns a JSON object with five fields and the engineer needs only one. Should the broadcast-join approach pre-fetch all five fields or only the one?
options: Pre-fetch all five fields and let the join project the one needed; the additional storage is negligible at 16 rows and the team has the option to use the other fields without re-fetching them in a future iteration of the pipeline.

Pre-fetch only the one field needed and let downstream pipelines pre-fetch their own fields if they want different ones; this keeps each pipeline's pre-fetch explicit and avoids a shared-table coupling between teams.

Pre-fetch all five fields but materialise them in a separate reference table that downstream pipelines can broadcast-join against; this turns the pre-fetch into a shared resource without coupling pipelines to one team's choice of fields.

Pre-fetch the one field needed but write a small wrapper that exposes all five so future pipelines can opt in without changing the pre-fetch logic; this lazy approach preserves both the minimum pre-fetch and the future flexibility.
fields.correctAnswer: Pre-fetch only the one field needed and let downstream pipelines pre-fetch their own fields if they want different ones; this keeps each pipeline's pre-fetch explicit and avoids a shared-table coupling between teams.
fields.rationale: The principle is to pre-fetch what is needed and let other consumers do the same.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Maximises future flexibility at the cost of present coupling; the storage argument is a footnote.
